comments.body:
Continued from the comment above: P1 to P3, and C1 to C4.

---

### P1. Replace personal data with a per-Target pseudonymous identifier

We agree that most requests don't need the person's email, and we share the privacy goal. We see the tracking risk a little differently, and that shaped the fix we're proposing.

A Target that receives hid.email doesn't learn where else that person has been. The token goes to one Target at a time, so it is a disclosure to that site, not a third-party cookie. The parties that can see traffic across many Targets are intermediaries, and fraud and account-takeover vendors already correlate their customers' traffic today by other means.

Your underlying concern still holds, though. An email address is a join key: a Target can match it against data it already holds or can buy, without anyone's help. And the token hands it over at the door, not at checkout. At checkout the merchant collects the name, email and addresses anyway, so the token adds little there. At the door, what the site needs to know is that a verified, accountable person stands behind the agent, and sub and the assurance claims already tell it that.

So we're changing the default. By default, hid will carry only hid.id, a pseudonymous identifier assigned by the issuer, together with the assurance claims. Email, phone number and name are added only when a Target needs them for a stated purpose, such as creating an account or checking out, and the person has agreed. The draft will say that an issuer MUST NOT include them without that authorization. The issuer can collect it or delegate that to the agent platform, and whoever collects it must be able to prove it. A Target asks for them through the decline response (your point C4), and later through a discovery document, so an agent can get it right the first time. Recognising a returning customer becomes the merchant's choice rather than something every token carries.

As you suggested, hid.id is per Target. It's unique to one person, on one agent platform, for one Target service, and it stays the same each time that person's agent comes back to that service. sub and aid.id work the same way. Two Targets can't match the values they receive, and neither can an intermediary that sees both.

The one part of your suggestion we'd like to approach differently is the out-of-band lookup. The security vendors we've spoken with work to very tight latency budgets and would rather not call an issuer in the request path. Avoiding that call is what makes Section 6.3 workable for a bot manager. So we'd like the token on its own to always be enough to admit a request. A party that has onboarded with the issuer can still call it when it wants more, but the drafts won't require it.

We also looked at giving each participant its own view of the token. On a single request, the CDN, bot manager, WAF, fraud tool and origin all read the same token, and Section 3.4 relies on that shared view. A separate token per layer would mean minting, signing and validating one for every hop. Selective disclosure (SD-JWT, which Section 9.1 mentions) doesn't quite fit either. It's selective per presentation, and a KYAPay request is one presentation that every hop sees. Where a Target's vendor runs on its own host, though, the agent can send that host a separate token, carrying only the claims the Target declared for it and the Target's own identifiers. That's a separate request rather than a different view of the same one.

One other change. The published text says sub "MUST be pairwise unique within a given issuer". In OpenID Connect Core Section 8, pairwise means a different value for each relying party. That isn't what our implementation did: sub was the same for a given person, platform and agent at every Target, and our editor's copy had dropped the word for that reason. With this change the word is accurate again, so it stays, and the definition will spell out what it means: a different sub for each Target, stable for that Target.

For completeness, here is what can still link Targets. apd identifies the agent platform, which is a business, so it stays the same everywhere, as do the agent's product name and the issuer. Identifying claims link wherever they're disclosed, which is why they now need a stated purpose and the person's agreement. Recognising the same person across Targets, which a cross-merchant fraud network depends on, would need the issuer's cooperation. The token alone won't allow it.

We'll carry two related changes into the drafts. Section 6.11 currently ties cross-channel linkage to a stable hid. It will say instead that hid.id, sub and aid.id are per Target, and that identifying claims appear only where a Target asked for them. And Section 9.1 will include a non-normative example of an admission decision made from sub, hid.id and the assurance claims, with no identifying claims, so issuers have a concrete model to follow. We'd rather not prescribe a claim set per layer, since deployments vary a lot. Section 9.1's "least revealing set sufficient for the decision at hand" seems like the right rule.

---

### P2. Keep payment data out of the token

We agree that seeing a KYAPay token should never bring a hop into PCI scope, and we'll take your MUST NOT, made a little more specific.

Token -02 already forbids a PAN (Sections 3.4.1 and 3.4.2) and requires token_security_code to be a single-use cryptogram, not a static CVV. Your sentence goes further: it covers every token type and all card data. We'd list what that means so it can be tested: "A token defined in this specification MUST NOT contain a Primary Account Number, full magnetic-stripe or chip track data, a static card verification value (CVV, CVC2 or CVV2), or a PIN or PIN block." We'll put it in Section 3.4.2 in place of the narrower rule there, rather than add a third statement.

On the hops: the card credential in sti is a payment token issued by the card network under the EMV Payment Tokenisation Specification. It is used with a single-use cryptogram, and the network restricts it to the merchant, amount and time window bound in the token. PCI SSC FAQ 1326 covers this case. For entities other than Token Service Providers, which includes every hop here, it says: "A Payment Token that is defined and used in accordance with the EMV Payment Tokenisation Specification and that exists outside of the Token Service Provider's token data environment is not considered Account Data and is therefore not in scope for PCI DSS." The draft says "PCI-exempt" today without a citation, so we'll replace that with the properties and the FAQ, and its limit: a system that also handles a PAN, or is connected to one that does, stays in scope.

That's also why we'd keep the credential in sti rather than use a reference the Target redeems. If the credential isn't Account Data, a reference leaves each hop holding the same thing in PCI terms, and it adds a redemption call and a dependency on the issuer at checkout. It would also need a merchant integration: today the agent puts the credential into the merchant's ordinary card fields, and the merchant authorizes it like any card. If you read FAQ 1326 differently, we'd like to hear it, since this rests on it.

Agreed that amt, cur and mnr stay.

Your comment also made us look at the examples. payment_token is "1234567890123456" and token_security_code is "123", which read like a card number and a CVV. We'll change both and label them as examples.

Changes, all in the token draft:

**1. Section 3.4.2, first two paragraphs replaced** (the third, on instruments within PCI DSS scope, stays):

Before:

> This specification supports card settlement only through payment-network agentic-commerce programmes that issue transaction-scoped, PCI-exempt credentials.
>
> A PAY or KYA-PAY token MUST NOT carry a Primary Account Number, or the static verification value associated with one.

After:

> This specification supports card settlement only through payment-network agentic-commerce programmes whose credentials are Payment Tokens as defined by the EMV Payment Tokenisation Specification [EMVCo-PT], used with a single-use token cryptogram and restricted by the payment network to the transaction bound in the token.
>
> A token defined in this specification, of any type, MUST NOT contain a Primary Account Number, full magnetic-stripe or chip track data, a static card verification value (CVV, CVC2 or CVV2), or a PIN or PIN block.

**2. Section 3.4.1, the paragraph on card credentials, last two sentences**:

Before:

> Such a credential is provisioned for a single transaction and is scoped to one initiator, one target, and one amount. It is not a Primary Account Number (PAN), and it cannot be used to derive the underlying PAN or the network's agentic token.

After:

> Such a credential is a payment token issued by the payment network (Section 3.4.2). It is used with a single-use token cryptogram (token_security_code), and the network restricts its use to one initiator, one target, and one amount. It is not a Primary Account Number (PAN), and the underlying PAN cannot feasibly be recovered from it.

**3. Section 5.3, both paragraphs replaced:**

Before:

> The sti claim of a PAY or KYA-PAY token carries a settlement instrument. When stp is card, that instrument is a network-issued agentic payment credential provisioned for a single transaction, accompanied by a single-use dynamic cryptogram. Such credentials are issued outside the scope of PCI DSS and cannot be used to derive the underlying account number.
>
> Implementations MUST NOT place a Primary Account Number, or a static Card Verification Value, in the sti claim. Doing so would place the token, and every system that processes it, within PCI DSS scope, for which this specification provides no confidentiality mechanism.

After:

> The sti claim of a PAY or KYA-PAY token carries a settlement instrument. When stp is card, that instrument is a payment token issued by a payment network and accompanied by a single-use token cryptogram (Section 3.4.1).
>
> For entities other than Token Service Providers, a Payment Token that is defined and used in accordance with the EMV Payment Tokenisation Specification and that exists outside the Token Service Provider's token data environment is not Account Data and is not in scope for PCI DSS [PCI-FAQ-1326]. Receiving, inspecting, or forwarding a token defined in this specification therefore does not of itself bring a recipient within that scope. That determination concerns the payment token, not the recipient's wider environment: a system that also stores, processes, or transmits Account Data, or is connected to one that does, remains in scope.
>
> Section 3.4.2 prohibits Account Data in any token. A token that carried it would bring every system that processes it within PCI DSS scope, for which this specification provides no confidentiality mechanism.

**4. Section 5.2, last paragraph**: "the credential is transaction-scoped and its accompanying cryptogram is single-use" becomes "the network restricts the credential to the transaction bound in the token, and its accompanying cryptogram is single-use".

**5. Section 5.4**: "Agentic payment credentials and their associated token cryptograms are single-use and short-lived" becomes "The token cryptograms that accompany agentic payment credentials are single-use and short-lived".

**6. Examples, Sections 3.4.3 and 3.5:**

```
"payment_token": "0000000000000000", // Example only: a network-issued payment token, not a PAN
"token_security_code": "000", // Example only: a single-use cryptogram (DTVV or TAVV), not a CVV
```

**7. Informative references added:**

- [EMVCo-PT] EMVCo, "EMV Payment Tokenisation Specification: Technical Framework".
- [PCI-FAQ-1326] PCI Security Standards Council, "How does PCI DSS apply to EMVCo Payment Tokens?", FAQ 1326, May 2015, https://www.pcisecuritystandards.org/faqs/1326.

---

### P3. Make aid.creation_ip optional

We agree, and creation_ip will become OPTIONAL.

Nothing in the token draft validates it (it isn't used in Section 4), and mandating personal data that nothing checks doesn't fit the minimal-disclosure principle in Section 6. An issuer that includes it can still do so.

We'll also say what it's for when present: a diagnostic aid, and at most a weak corroborating signal, as Using Section 6.3 says.

For clarity, this is separate from source_ips, which says where an agent's requests to Targets will come from and is already OPTIONAL. creation_ip records where the token was requested from.

While we're there, we'll change the example addresses to documentation ranges.

Changes, all in the token draft:

**1. Section 3.3.3, creation_ip:**

Before:

> creation_ip: REQUIRED - The public IP address of the system / agent that requested the token. Its value is a string containing the public IPv4 or IPv6 address from where the token request originated. It MUST be captured directly from the token request.

After:

> creation_ip: OPTIONAL - The public IP address of the system / agent that requested the token. Its value is a string containing the public IPv4 or IPv6 address from where the token request originated. When present, it MUST be captured directly from the token request. It is a diagnostic aid, for example when investigating an incident, and is not an access-control signal: a recipient MAY use it as a weak corroborating signal only and MUST NOT treat it as sufficient on its own (Section 6.3 of [I-D.skyfire-oauth-using-kyapay-tokens]). It is personal data, subject to the privacy considerations in Section 6.

**2. Examples (Figure 1 in Section 3.3, Figure 3 in Section 3.5), aid:**

- `creation_ip`: `"54.86.50.139"` and `"128.2.42.95"` become `"192.0.2.10"` and `"198.51.100.20"` (RFC 5737). The comment "IP Address where token was created" becomes "IP address the token was requested from".
- `source_ips`: become `["192.0.2.10-192.0.2.12", "203.0.113.0/24", "2001:db8:abcd:12::/64", "agents.example.com"]` (RFC 5737, RFC 3849, RFC 2606).

---

### C1. Header grammar and Structured Fields disagree

We'll take your first option. The registration in Section 10.1 is the one we meant, so Section 5.1 will define the field as a Structured Field List and drop its own ABNF.

We'd make the members Tokens rather than Strings. A compact JWT uses only letters, digits, "-", "_" and ".", and always starts with a letter, so it's already a valid Token. That means the unquoted form senders use today stays valid, with nothing to change on the wire. RFC 9651 only requires parsers to handle Tokens of 512 characters, and many KYAPay tokens are longer, so the draft will also say recipients must handle members up to the field-size minimum under C2.

On a bad field, we'd reject the request. RFC 9651 Section 4.2 allows either ignoring the whole field or treating the message as malformed, so this is our choice rather than something the RFC settles. The same applies to a member that parses but isn't a well-formed JWT. We'd rather not process part of a credential.

Changes, all in the Using draft:

**1. Section 5.1, the ABNF and the paragraph after it replaced:**

Before:

> KYAPay-Token = token-jwt *( OWS "," OWS token-jwt ) token-jwt    = 1*( ALPHA / DIGIT / "-" / "_" / "." )
>
> A request MAY convey more than one token (for example, separate KYA and PAY tokens) either as a comma-separated list in a single KYAPay-Token header field or as multiple KYAPay-Token header fields; per Section 5.2 of [RFC9110], multiple field lines with the same name are equivalent to a single comma-separated field line. Because a JWT uses only the base64url alphabet plus the period (".") separator, it never contains a comma, so list parsing is unambiguous.

After:

> KYAPay-Token is a List Structured Field (Section 3.1 of [RFC9651]). Each member is a Token (Section 3.3.4 of [RFC9651]) whose value is a JWT in compact serialization, with no parameters. A compact JWT consists only of base64url characters and periods, and it begins with the encoding of a JSON object, so its first character is a letter; it is therefore a valid Token as it stands. For example:
>
> KYAPay-Token: eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6Imt5YStqd3QifQ.eyJpc3Mi...
>
> A request MAY convey more than one token (for example, separate KYA and PAY tokens), either as members of one field line or in several KYAPay-Token field lines, which are combined before parsing as described in Section 4.2 of [RFC9651].

**2. Section 5.1, the last recipient bullet replaced and two added:**

Before:

> * MUST ignore a KYAPay-Token member it cannot parse as a JWT, while continuing to process the remaining members, unless local policy requires rejecting the whole request.

After:

> * MUST parse the field as a List [RFC9651]. A field that fails to parse fails as a whole, and a recipient MUST NOT attempt to recover individual members from it;
>
> * MUST reject the request if the field fails to parse, or if any member is not a Token whose value is a well-formed JWT. Section 4.2 of [RFC9651] permits either ignoring a field that fails to parse or treating the message as malformed; this document requires the latter; and
>
> * MUST be able to parse members as long as the field value it is required to accept (the Token Size section), which exceeds the minimum Token length that [RFC9651] requires parsers to support.

**3. References:** add [RFC9651] to the normative references. The Using draft doesn't cite it today, although Section 10.1 registers the field as a Structured Field.

---

### C2. Header size

We agree the drafts need to say this. It's drafted in two pull requests, skyfire-xyz/draft-skyfire-oauth-kyapay-token#48 and #4 here, which we're tightening before they merge.

Rather than a maximum on senders, which can't be enforced and would make working deployments non-conforming, they set a minimum every recipient must accept: 6144 octets for the whole KYAPay-Token field value, however many tokens it carries. The token draft adds the issuer's side: limits on the total size of the claims, such that a token within them fits inside 6144, and a preference for one combined KYA-PAY token over separate KYA and PAY tokens in the same request.

6144 comes from the tightest limit on the path, which is the per-field limit at the origin web server, not the CDN or load balancer. 4096 is too small for a token carrying every registered claim, and 8192 plus the field name is over common origin defaults. A recipient that rejects an oversized field should return 431 rather than 400, so the sender can tell a size problem from a malformed token.

Since the field is now a List of Tokens (C1), recipients' parsers must also handle members of that size, because RFC 9651 only guarantees 512 characters.

You're right that P1 makes tokens smaller: by default hid carries only hid.id and the assurance claims. A typical token is already about a third of the minimum. The minimum is there for the tail, when a Target asks for identifying claims.

Changes (the two pull requests, condensed):

**1. Pull request #4 (this draft), the Token Size section, replaced by:**

> A recipient MUST accept a KYAPay-Token field value of at least 6144 octets. The minimum applies to the field value as a whole, however many tokens it carries, and a recipient's parser MUST accept List members of that length. A recipient MUST NOT truncate the field value, and MUST NOT treat a field it rejects for its size as absent. When it rejects a field for its size, it SHOULD respond with 431 (Request Header Fields Too Large) [RFC6585]. 6144 octets fits a token carrying every claim registered in [I-D.skyfire-oauth-kyapay-token] and stays within common origin-server limits for a single header field.

**2. skyfire-xyz/draft-skyfire-oauth-kyapay-token#48, the Token Size section, replaced by:**

> This specification sets no maximum token size; the Token Size section of [I-D.skyfire-oauth-using-kyapay-tokens] sets the minimum a recipient must accept. An issuer SHOULD NOT emit claims registered by this specification totalling more than 3072 octets of JSON, or other claims totalling more than 1024 octets. These limits apply to the claims before encoding. Base64url encoding adds about a third, so 4096 octets of claims, with a typical JOSE header and an ES256 signature, serializes to about 5670 octets, within that minimum. An issuer using a larger header or signature SHOULD check the complete serialized token against that minimum. Where a request would carry both a KYA token and a PAY token, an issuer SHOULD issue one KYA-PAY token instead, because two tokens at these limits exceed a single header field at a typical origin.

**3. C1's third recipient bullet** becomes: "MUST accept List members as long as the field value it is required to accept (the Token Size section)."

---

### C3. Browser agents and CORS

You're right that Section 3.3 claims more than it should, and we'll scope it.

On page scripts, agreed. A custom header on a cross-origin fetch triggers a preflight, and page script can't send it unless the Target allows it in Access-Control-Allow-Headers. That is work for the merchant, and Section 3.3 doesn't say so.

On browser-use agents, our experience is different. An agent that controls the browser can add header fields at the network layer, below the page, and they then appear on the requests the browser sends: navigations, sub-resources, fetch and XHR. We tested this with Chrome 154 driven by Playwright. The field was present on a stylesheet, an image, fetch and XMLHttpRequest, and no preflight was sent, because the browser decides on a preflight from the request the page built, before the field is added. The exception we found was requests made by a service worker.

So the line isn't browser versus non-browser. It's whether the party attaching the token controls the request's header fields. We'd scope Section 3.3 on that, without describing browser mechanics, since those change faster than the draft will.

On which requests carry the token: any kind of request can, whether a page load, a sub-resource or an API call. What decides it is where the request goes.
- **The Target:** its own requests carry its token.
- **Hosts acting for the Target**, such as its other hosts or a captcha or fraud vendor: each gets a token that names the Target and carries only the claims set for that host. By default that is hid.id and the assurance claims, with no other personal data and no payment data. Payment details go to such a host only where it is set up to receive them, for example a payment provider handling checkout for the Target.
- **Other hosts** shouldn't get a token at all, and never more than that default.

For now, which hosts act for a Target, and what each gets, is configured. Later the Target will be able to declare it. We'd put this in a new Section 5.4 rather than list request types in 5.1, since a list would date. It also refines the S7 text, so the two sections agree.

Two related additions to Section 5.1:
- a preflight doesn't carry the field, so a recipient shouldn't treat one as a request without a token;
- a response that depends on the field must carry Vary: KYAPay-Token and must not be stored by shared caches. RFC 9111's protection for authenticated responses is keyed on Authorization, so it doesn't cover a custom field. Without this, a CDN could serve one agent's response to another.

Changes, all in the Using draft:

**1. Section 3.3, appended after the last sentence:**

> This holds where the party attaching the token controls the header fields of the request that reaches the Target. Where it does not, the token is conveyed by another binding (Section 5.2) or the interaction does not use this header field.

**2. New Section 5.4, "Attaching Tokens to Requests":**

> How an agent attaches a token to a request is an implementation matter, for the reasons given in Section 7. Any kind of request may carry a KYAPay-Token field; whether it does, and which token it carries, depends on where the request is sent:
>
> * A request to the Target carries the token requested for that Target.
>
> * A Target may rely on other hosts, such as its own hosts in other domains or vendors acting on its behalf. A request to such a host carries a token that names the Target in its audience claims (Section 5.3) and carries the claims that apply to that host, which may include payment claims. Where no claims are set for the host, the token carries only the base claims: hid limited to its id member and assurance claims, apd, and aid without creation_ip, with no payment claims. Where the claims for the host match those of the Target's token, the agent MAY send the Target's token.
>
> * A request to any other host SHOULD NOT carry a token. If it does, the token MUST NOT carry more than the base claims.
>
> The Target determines which hosts act on its behalf and which claims each receives. Until a mechanism exists for the Target to declare this, an agent learns it by configuration or from an arrangement with the Target.

**3. Section 5.1, appended:**

> A CORS preflight request does not carry the KYAPay-Token field: the user agent sends it to ask whether the field may be sent. A recipient MUST NOT apply its token-absent policy to a preflight request.
>
> Where a response depends on the KYAPay-Token field, the response MUST include Vary: KYAPay-Token and MUST be marked so that shared caches do not store it, for example with Cache-Control: private. The protection in Section 3.5 of [RFC9111] applies only to requests that carry the Authorization field.

**4. Section 8.6 (approved under S7), the attachment sentence:**

Before (as approved under S7):

> Agents SHOULD attach a token only to requests sent to the Target for which the token was requested; where the token carries tdm, that means a destination within the domain that tdm names.

After:

> Agents SHOULD attach tokens only as Section 5.4 describes: the token requested for a Target only to requests sent to that Target (where the token carries tdm, a destination within the domain that tdm names), and to any other host no more than the claims that apply to it.

(The next sentence, "The component that attaches a token MUST make that decision without relying on model output", is unchanged.)

**5. References:** add [RFC9111], informative.

---

### C4. No challenge or error response

We agree there's a gap: a Target needs to be able to say that a token is required, that the one it got was refused, or that it needs more than the token carries. We'd rather not reuse RFC 9470, though, and for the last case we don't think a challenge fits.

RFC 9470 is built for OAuth access tokens. Its error is defined in terms of "the access token presented with the request", and the client behaviour it prescribes is a redirect to an authorization server. A KYAPay agent has no authorization server to go back to, so a client following it would loop.

Step-up in OAuth also works because a person is there and only has to sign in again. Here, "needs more" can mean an attribute the person hasn't agreed to share, which takes seconds, or one the issuer hasn't verified yet, which can take minutes to days. That's a decline that says what's required, rather than a challenge.

So we'd respond with 403, or 402 where what's missing is payment, and add a response field, Accept-KYAPay-Token. It follows Accept-Signature in RFC 9421: it says what the next request needs, for example which claims and for what purpose. The reason can go in a problem details body (RFC 9457). An agent can tell the three cases apart from the field and what it sent. The draft will give the structure and examples, and leave the actual requirements to each Target, since KYAPay is used in too many settings for us to define them all. Later, a Target will also be able to publish the same requirements in advance, so an agent gets the token right the first time.

We wouldn't use 401: HTTP requires a 401 to carry a WWW-Authenticate challenge, and a KYAPay token isn't an Authorization credential.

On why a new request header rather than an Authorization scheme: agreed, the draft should say. Clashing with the site's own authentication is one reason. The token also isn't a credential for the Target's resources, and the same token travels over transports other than HTTP, where Authorization has no meaning. We'll add that to Section 5.1.

Changes, all in the Using draft:

**1. Section 6.5 replaced. New title "Responding When a Token Falls Short":**

> A recipient can decline a request because it carries no KYAPay token, because the token fails validation (Section 6.1), or because the token is valid but does not carry what the action requires: for example identity claims, a higher assurance level for a sensitive action, or a payment token. Not all actions carry the same risk; viewing a loyalty balance is far less sensitive than making a large payment, and a token attests only the assurance established when it was issued.
>
> In each case the recipient responds with 403 (Forbidden), or with 402 (Payment Required) where what is missing or insufficient is payment, and SHOULD include the Accept-KYAPay-Token field (Section 5.5) stating what a request needs in order to succeed. A recipient SHOULD NOT use 401 (Unauthorized) for these cases: that status requires a WWW-Authenticate challenge (Section 15.5.2 of [RFC9110]), and a KYAPay token is not an Authorization credential. A recipient MAY describe the reason in a problem details body [RFC9457].
>
> An agent that receives such a response can compare it with what it sent. If it sent no token, or a token that was refused, it can obtain a new token and retry. If the token lacked something the recipient requires, obtaining it may involve the human principal, for example to agree to share an attribute or to complete further verification with the issuer, which can take minutes to days.
>
> The same requirements can also be published in advance, so that an agent obtains a suitable token the first time. This document does not define how.

**2. New Section 5.5, "The Accept-KYAPay-Token Response Field"** (after C3's §5.4):

> Accept-KYAPay-Token is a Dictionary Structured Field (Section 3.2 of [RFC9651]) that a recipient sends in a response to state what a request needs to carry for the recipient to accept it. Each member states one requirement. The member's key is a label chosen by the recipient. Its value is an Inner List of Strings, each naming a claim, using the claim names of [I-D.skyfire-oauth-kyapay-token] with a period between a claim and its sub-claim (for example, "hid.email").
>
> Parameters on a member qualify the requirement. Uses of KYAPay vary too widely for this document to define a complete set, so recipients define the parameters and values they need. Two that are commonly useful are:
>
> * purpose: a Token saying why the recipient needs the claims, which an agent can show to the human principal when asking for consent; and
>
> * optional: a Boolean; when true, the recipient would like the claims but does not require them.
>
> For example:
>
> Accept-KYAPay-Token: checkout=("hid.email");purpose=checkout, fraud=("hid.phone_number");purpose=fraud_prevention;optional
>
> A recipient that requires payment names payment claims in the same way, for example pay=("amt" "cur");purpose=checkout.
>
> An agent MUST ignore parameters it does not recognize. A recipient that responds to cross-origin requests MUST list Accept-KYAPay-Token in Access-Control-Expose-Headers, so that a browser-based agent can read it.

**3. Section 5.1, appended:**

> KYAPay tokens are carried in a dedicated header field rather than in Authorization. A Target commonly uses Authorization for its own authentication; a KYAPay token is not a credential for access to the Target's resources; and the same token is carried over transports other than HTTP (Section 5.2), where Authorization has no meaning. For the same reasons, a recipient states its requirements in the Accept-KYAPay-Token response field (Section 5.5) rather than in a WWW-Authenticate challenge.

**4. Section 10.1, a second registration:**

> * Field Name: Accept-KYAPay-Token
> * Status: permanent
> * Structured Type: Dictionary
> * Reference: Section 5.5 of this document
> * Comments: States what a request must carry for a KYAPay recipient to accept it

**5. References:** add [RFC9457], informative.

---

That's everything. We'll link the pull requests here as they go up, and we'd welcome your review on them.

Ankit

Summary of Changes
This PR updates the architectural characterization of Bot Management Systems across §2.1, §3.4, and §6.3 of draft-skyfire-oauth-using-kyapay-tokens-00. It shifts the definition of bot managers from network/transport-layer filters (L3/L4) to inline application-layer (L7) systems.
Additionally, it reframes §6.3 around agent self-identification and policy-driven disposition:
Self-Identification Over Detection: Presenting a valid KYA token allows an agent to explicitly self-identify as automated up front. This settles the identification question and allows the bot manager to bypass redundant behavioral telemetry and fingerprinting heuristics.
Decoupling Identification from Admission: Token verification provides authenticated context (hid, apd, aid), but leaves admission as a site-configured policy decision (admit, rate-limit,  deny) rather than a mandated bypass.

reviews.body: Revised: KYAPay tokens replace network-level inference with un-forgeable, issuer-signed assertions. Signed by a trusted issuer and verified against public keys, the token can carry the agent instance (aid), the execution platform (apd), and the identified principal the issuer asserts the agent acts for (hid). Where network indicators only establish that a request comes from a known operator's network, a KYAPay token establishes that a specific agent is acting for a specific, verified subscriber.

comments.body: My understanding is that the WWW-Authenticate response assumes a human is present. It is supposed to trigger a browser window for the human to resolve the challenge immediately. This will likely not be possible with agents as the human may not be around, the agent may be running in the cloud somewhere, etc. In the discovery draft, I was going to propose a specific but distinct header response that would not overlap with this established behavior if the www-authenticate header. WDYT?
Not true - it's non interactive. See the use of WWW-Authenticate by DPoP, for instance.

I see it. Thanks for pointing it out. Another question though as I dug deeper
- Is the WWW-Authenticate response header meant to be paired with the Authorization request header? Since KYA Tokens have their own request header, does it make sense to have its own response header?
-- For example, HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421) hit the same problem. It defines its own Accept-Signature header for asking for a signature, not WWW-Authenticate.

We could follow HTTP Signatures precedent.  That said, https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#name-www-authenticate says:
> A server generating a [401 (Unauthorized)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#status.401) response MUST send a WWW-Authenticate header field containing at least one challenge. A server MAY generate a WWW-Authenticate header field in other response messages to indicate that supplying credentials (or different credentials) might affect the response.

So if a 401 is returned, we're expected to provide WWW-Authenticate.

This is unrelated to the main purpose of the PR, which is to update the introduction with more precise information on traditional bot detection methods.  That part of the PR is mature and ready to merge.

@dsenecal26, I suggest that we file an issue to discuss the right syntax to use for handling particular kinds of errors.  Given we're in OAuth, the first choice would be to use the OAuth error syntax from RFC 6749.  But if we're returning information about what it will take to authorize a request, I believe that we should be using WWW-Authenticate.

Do we have to follow the RFC's exact format?
WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="simple", Newauth realm="apps", type=1, title="Login to \"apps\""

Or is the value flexible, in which case we could go for:
WWW-Authenticate: Error = "KYA Token required", Preferred issuer = "https://prefered-token-issuer-url_1, https://prefered-token-issuer-url_2”

Yes - when we use an RFC, we have to use it in a conformant manner.

Realm isn't required.  Having an authentication method, is.  See https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#name-www-authenticate for the definition.

I have to think about whether we can use WWW-Authenticate when we don't have a corresponding "Authentication" value like "Basic".  Of course, we could make one up, like "KYAPay".  Then we'd still be using the WWW-Authenticate syntax correctly.

I worry that using WWW-Authenticate response header will confuse developers and they will assume that the KYAPay token is sent in the Authorization request header. I think we should follow RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures on this. That RFC does not pick specific HTTP response status codes. It just specifies the request headers "Signature-Input" and "Signature" and the response header "Accept-Signature".

We could follow the same pattern - "KYAPay-Token" and "Accept-KYAPay-Token" and not be prescriptive on the  response status codes at all. Or if you feel strongly that we must use HTTP status codes in addition to the response header, then we could limit ourselves to 400 and/or 403 with 402 reserved for payment related issues. This would take 401 out of the mix and remove the requirement for WWW-Authenticate.

Another thought:  An alternative to completely deleting the 6.3 content is to have it describe the kinds of error that would be likely to be returned but to remove the syntax for the errors and say that the best syntax is still being determined.
